newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - The shares drama fades.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - The shares drama fades.

text.p: The conflict-of-interest drama, which seemed so critical on Wednesday morning, is now clearly fading away.
The government has survived the crisis with only moderate damage: it has lost a junior minister, a parliamentary secretary and presumably some undetermined voter support.
Unless some new revelations emerge, perhaps from Thursday's question time in parliament, the Labor opposition will be unable to maintain media attention on the issue.

It was dying on Wednesday afternoon, even after Trade Minister Tim Fischer admitted that he had only just got rid of his shares in BHP, whose interests he had had to promote as part of his ministerial duties.

The only kick-along to emerge so far on Thursday was The Australian Financial Review's report that the share interest that Finance Minister John Fahey had failed to declare in federal parliament had been declared in New South Wales state parliament last year.
But that is triviality, and the related misleading of parliament carries little weight, too.
Consider this:
-- The company, which supplied office services to Fahey's former legal partnership 10 years ago, is utterly unimportant.
-- He no longer even owns his share in it.
Sure, he should have had all the records correct, as he admits. But the issue should be beneath federal politics.
There are more important issues to discuss.
Fisher and especially Industry Minister John Moore have not come out of this smelling so sweetly.
But there is no chorus calling for their resignations and the bottom line is that it is all seems to be blowing over.
Perhaps Prime Minister John Howard summarised the week best on Sydney radio 2UE on Thursday morning:
"It has been technically messy.
"A number of people have been careless.
"I am less than amused at that because they have embarrassed my government and I regret that and I apologise to the Australian people for that having occurred.
"But there has been no evidence of deliberate dishonesty. There's been no evidence of personal gain. There's been no evidence that people have taken a dollar.
"If there had been then I would have freely acknowledged it.
"But it doesn't alter the fact that a couple of people have been less than careful and they deserve some of the embarrassment they suffered.

"But I regret very much that it has embarrassed my government and the people of Australia are entitled and your listeners are entitled to have from me an apology for the embarrassement that they have caused the government.
"And I can assure you that the events of this week will not be forgotten by quite a number of people."
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
